A year ago, on November 21 2025, the government noti- ﬁed the labour Codes, mark- ing one of India’s most comprehensive labour reforms since Independence. Nearly ﬁve years after Parlia- ment passed the Codes in 2019-2020, the government moved towards implementa- tion, having engaged with stakeholders in the interven- ing period to undertake pre- paratory work and clarify key provisions. With the focus now shifting to execu- tion, it is timely to take stock of the progress made during the ﬁrst year and con- sider what more needs to be done to ensure that the reforms deliver their intended outcomes. A signiﬁcant develop- ment, ﬁrst and foremost, has been the progress towards a common regulatory frame- work, replacing the complex web of statutes and com- pliance requirements that historically discouraged business expansion. While addressing stakeholder con- cerns is an ongoing process, a near-uniform acceptance of the codes is evident. From notiﬁcation to operationalisation of rules Following notiﬁcation, sev- eral procedural and com- pliance provisions of the Codes required detailed rules. Therefore, the govern- ment published the draft Central rules under all four Codes on 30 December 2025, inviting stakeholder com- ments and suggestions. Fol- lowing the consultation process, ﬁnal Central rules under all four Codes were notiﬁed in May 2026. With labour on the con- current list, states and union territories must also notify rules within their jurisdic- tions. At the state level, the process of framing and notifying corresponding rules has progressed at vary- ing speeds. While some states and union territories have notiﬁed ﬁnal rules under all four Codes, others are at ﬁnal stages of rule-making. Digital compliance and ease of doing business Digital compliance is a key driver of ease of doing busi- ness (EoDB). The labour min- istry has launched the revamped Shram Suvidha 2.0 portal in recent months, enabling businesses to obtain a single registration, secure a single licence and ﬁle a single return, thereby simplifying compliance across labour authorities. A pragmatic approach appears to allow states to retain their existing digital compliance systems rather than requiring their integra- tion into a single Central portal. For businesses operat- ing across multiple states, Shram Suvidha is expected to serve as a common interface for coordinated compliance and time-bound approvals. Building a wider social security ecosystem Importantly, the labour Codes lay the foundation for extending social security coverage to unorganised, gig and platform workers. In a signiﬁcant step towards oper- ationalising this framework, the Union govern- ment, on 30 October 2026, notiﬁed the con- stitution of two separate National Social Security Boards — one for unor- ganised workers and the other for gig and platform workers. The Boards are mandated to recommend, advise on and monitor welfare schemes for these categories of workers, thereby paving the way for more inclusive social security coverage and strengthening the formalisa- tion of India’s workforce. Further, the e-Shram portal’s aggregator module continues to facilitate the reg- istration and integration of platform workers into the social security framework, representing an important dimension of extending social security coverage to the gig and platform economy. What has changed for workers and businesses? As implementation prog- resses, the labour Codes are beginning to deliver tangible beneﬁts for workers and businesses. For workers, a key reform is the uniform deﬁnition of wages, estab- lishing a minimum 50 per cent wage base for calculat- ing social security contribu- tions and other statutory beneﬁts. Industry practi- tioners indicate that most large enterprises have undertaken wage restructur- ing and made necessary ﬁnancial provisions. Two other illustrative indications from the ﬁeld concern maternity beneﬁts and payment of wages. In both areas, the Codes have expanded the Central government’s jurisdiction. Increased repre- sentations reportedly received by Central labour authorities in these areas sug- gest greater awareness and use of these mechanisms. Apart from digital com- pliance mechanisms being in place, the inspector-cum- facilitator system deﬁned under the Codes brings relief to businesses. It seeks to replace the traditional inspec- tion-heavy approach with risk-based oversight, digital reporting and an emphasis on self-compliance. EPFO reforms and expansion of formal social security Meanwhile, the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) has strengthened the formal social security frame- work by notifying its schemes in June 2026. Effec- tive 17 September 2026, the mandatory EPFO wage ceil- ing also increased from ~15,000 to ~25,000 per month, extending provident fund, pension and insurance coverage to more employees. Additionally, the VISH- WAS and AMNESTY schemes, notiﬁed in June 2026, signal a shift towards facilitation rather than enforcement alone. What stakeholders expect next Stakeholders may continue to require handholding, clar- ity and predictability in the implementation process for some time. Key priorities would include timely state- level notiﬁcations, effective grievance redressal mechan- isms, operationalisation of the ﬂoor wage framework, a single point of contact for resolving EPF-related issues, early notiﬁcation of social security schemes for the unorganised sector, to name a few. Representatives of the construction industry have suggested an integrated labour database or a ‘labour stack’ that could play a criti- cal role in enabling portabil- ity of beneﬁts, ensuring continuity of coverage and preventing duplication. The road ahead: From reform to delivery Ultimately, the Codes’ suc- cess will be measured by out- comes, some of these being: Wage related, greater female labour force participation, safer workplaces, greater for- malisation of India’s labour market, a predictable com- pliance environment with enhanced transparency and simpliﬁcation of processes for greater EoDB. vvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvvv The writer is a former Union labour secretary.
